title: Was Duke's notation a secret shorthand?
summary: Willard asks about Duke's musical shorthand; Tizol says Duke wrote whatever sounded right to him, for his players' sounds, and relays Duke's remark that mistakes can be the best part.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: So there wasn't any big secret about it? Somebody -- I think it was either Herbie Jones or Jimmie Jones, who said that Duke had his own kind of musical shorthand; almost like a code that he wrote in -- that somebody who didn't know him or didn't work with him, wouldn't understand what he wanted.

Well, I don't know. I remember one time I heard him say -- he sat down at the piano, and he said if that sounds good to him, he's gonna write it -- I don't care even if the harmony was wrong. He would write whatever he thinks is gonna sound all right to him. And his chords, and That is why he got away, on account of the way the band sounded many times, because he was writing for Like Tricky Sam -- who could write for Tricky Sam? the musicians in the way they played their horns. That's the way he did it. Oh, he was a hell of a nice fellow; and people don't realize it --he did so many good things with that pencil.
I know ... somebody said in a rehearsal, "Oh, I played that wrong", and Duke said, "Don't change it -- the mistakes are the best part!"
